First person POV stepping out of a cybernetic Mongolian ger, one hand pulling back a sun bleached felt flap threaded with fiber optics. Camera tilts up into a cobalt sky crowded with drones at every altitude. A battered cargo octocopter passes overhead carrying a folded solar array, carbon fiber arms sharp against a white thunderhead. Higher up, relay drones glint like migrating birds. Below, thousands of gers form a sprawling cyberpunk steppe settlement. Black solar panels fan from rooftops; horse drawn carts carry GPU towers, transparent coolant hoses, hand soldered power boards. Flexible antenna masts bow in wind; orange cables run through tall grass. At camp's edge, riders fold panels onto wagons and head west, blue drones trailing into open country. Ultra wide 70mm film still, sky filling upper two thirds, hard midday shadows, vivid summer greens, polished silicon beside patched felt and scarred aluminum, heat haze over distant tents.

Operation Legacy was a programme of the British Colonial Office (later Foreign Office) to destroy or hide files that would implicate the British Empire in wrongdoing, as to prevent them from being used by their ex-colonies.[1][2][3] It ran from the 1950s until the 1970s, when the decolonisation of the British Empire was at its height,[4] and involved at least 23 countries.[5]

Methods of operation
MI5 or Special Branch agents were required to vet all secret documents in the colonial administrations to find those that could "embarrass" Britain or show "racial prejudice or religious bias".[5] Some 8,800 files were consequently stored in Britain.[5] Precise instructions were given for methods to be used for destruction, including burning and dumping at sea.[5] Some of the files detailed torture methods used against opponents of the colonial administrations, such as during the Mau Mau Uprising.[6]

As decolonisation progressed, British officials were keen to avoid a repeat of the embarrassment that had been caused by the overt burning of documents[7] that took place in New Delhi in 1946, which had been covered by Indian news sources. On 3 May 1961, Iain Macleod, who was Secretary of State for the Colonies, wrote a telegram to all British embassies to advise them on the best way to retrieve and dispose of sensitive documents.[4] To prevent post-colonial governments from ever learning about Operation Legacy, officials were required to dispatch "destruction certificates" to London. In some cases, as the handover date approached, the immolation task proved so huge that colonial administrators warned the Foreign Office that there was a danger of "celebrating Independence Day with smoke".[8]

Thousands of cyber-Mongolian horse archers ride west in mass formation beneath a deep cobalt sky, their horses’ GPU fans stirring up snow. Far ahead, an isolated post hangs over the basin as a single luminous pane. The lead rider stands in the stirrups and shoots an arrow carrying a tiny glass copy of the pane. Hundreds of riders wheel away in formation, shooting copies toward distant camps. On the far horizon, camp after camp lights up as the quotes arrive. In the foreground, a rider hangs low off the saddle to pluck a fallen reply from the snow. A few blue butterflies scatter in the horses’ wake. The image has two panels sharing a time axis from 2:00 to 2:21, titled “12 In the Hall of the Mountain King.”

The top panel shows loudness in decibels, from 0 at the top to −60 at the bottom, as a filled orange area. The track stays near full volume, but it is broken by a series of sharp dips and sudden recoveries:

2:00–2:04: Near 0 dB, sliding gradually to about −15 dB.
2:04: A sharp spike, then a decay.
2:05.5: Volume jumps back to about −10 dB.
2:08: A peak near 0 dB, falling to about −25 dB just before 2:09.
2:09: A sudden attack, a decay, then a return to around −5 dB from 2:10 to 2:13.
2:13.5: A brief dip.
2:14: A spike to 0 dB, followed by the deepest fall, to about −40 dB at 2:15.
2:15: An abrupt return to loud, sustained sound until about 2:17.
2:17–2:20: A drop to about −20 dB, then a steady crescendo back to near 0 dB around 2:20.
2:21: The volume tapers to about −27 dB.

The bottom panel is a mel-scale spectrogram. Pitch runs from 0 to above 8,192 Hz on the vertical axis, and intensity runs from black (silent) through purple to bright orange and yellow (loud). The strongest energy sits below about 1,000 Hz, with the brightest band in the deep bass. The loud passages fill the full frequency range in dense orange texture with faint horizontal harmonic lines. Each dip in loudness shows up as a dark vertical gap where the high frequencies vanish first, tapering into wedge shapes near 2:05, 2:10, and 2:15. Between 2:15 and 2:17, regular vertical stripes suggest a pounding, repeated rhythm. After 2:17, everything above roughly 1,000 Hz goes black. The upper edge of the sound then climbs in a smooth curve back to about 8,000 Hz by 2:20, like a filter slowly opening, before the full spectrum returns at the very end.

Sheet music for piano titled “Schleptet in E-flat (Mostly) on a Theme by TheFatRat, S. 627½.” It is written in E-flat major and 4/4 time, and marked “Allegro, mostly.” The piece goes wrong almost at once. In measure 1, the right hand starts off briskly, but an “oops” marks a stray C-sharp while the left hand hasn’t come in yet. In measure 2, the right hand holds one long note, marked “(confused),” while the left hand finally enters with a scramble of sharps and naturals labeled “in the wrong key.” Measures 3 and 4 slip into the tune of “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star,” marked “(that’s Mozart’s),” over a bass line labeled “oom pah.” Measure 5, marked “(stuck),” repeats the same tiny sixteenth-note figure four times over unchanging eighth notes. Then the piece can’t stop ending. Measure 6 cadences and asks “Fine?” Measure 7 cadences again: “Fine.” Measure 8 hits two lone chords separated by rests: “No, really. Fine.” Measure 9 is a single whole note held under a fermata, marked “(for TheFatRat),” but it’s a D, not the home note of E-flat, so the piece ends one step short of resolving while the left hand rests.

Sheet music for piano titled “Variation XII (Finale) on a Theme by TheFatRat, K. 627.” It is written on a treble and bass staff in E-flat major (three flats), in 4/4 time, and marked Allegro. The right hand plays almost continuous sixteenth notes: quick figures that rock back and forth between neighboring notes, then dip down in short turns. Measures 2 and 4 climb briefly to a higher register before settling back. In measure 5, the melody runs down quickly from a high note, lands on a held note, and then flutters between two notes in rapid thirty-second notes. The left hand plays steady eighth notes that leap between low and higher chord tones throughout. The sixth and final measure slows to quarter and half notes, with both hands landing on E-flat for a final cadence, followed by a double bar line.
